system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2138-05-21 22:35:00 to 2138-05-22 19:34:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD, and migraines was admitted for evaluation of recurrent atypical chest pain, dizziness, and a new-onset headache. The chest pain was brief, sharp, and radiated to the back, but cardiac workup including EKG, troponins, and CTA chest was negative for acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection. Dizziness was attributed to poor oral intake and improved with IV fluids. The headache was consistent with her migraine history and resolved with supportive care. She was started on Inderal LA for migraine prophylaxis. Her chronic conditions remained stable on home medications. Given the absence of organic pathology and improvement in symptoms, she was discharged home with follow-up instructions.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with chest pain and dizziness. 
 You had an ECG which had some small changes compared to priors 
however not concerning for a heart attack.  You had a chest xray 
which did not appear to show any signs of infection/ pneumonia.  
You had lab tests which showed no evidence of heart problems as 
well.  You were monitored on telemetry to make sure your heart 
rate was regular, which it was.  Your vital signs were checked 
frequently and were stable.

Because your dizziness is so closely related to when you sit up 
or stand up, we think this is most likely orthostatic 
hypotension.  In other words, your blood pressure likely goes a 
little bit low for a brief time when you sit or stand up.  This 
is most likely because you are dehydrated as you haven't been 
eating or drinking much.  Please try to drink at least 4 large 
cups (or 8 small cups) of water daily.  Also, do your best to 
eat 3 meals per day.  You may also have small snacks frequently 
if you prefer.

After speaking with you, it seems that the sadness that you are 
experiencing may be contributing to your symptoms of chest pain 
and taking away some of your desire to eat and drink.  I think 
it is important that you continue to follow up with your 
psychiatrist and try to initiate in home couseling services (per 
your discussion with ___ from our social work service)

We held a few of your medications while you were in the hospital 
since you were getting dizzy when sitting up.  These include 
spironolactone, lisinopril, and amlodipine.  You should continue 
to take your lisinopril, and amlodipine as you were before 
coming in.  We decreased the dose of your spironolactone to 50mg 
twice a day ___ pill twice per day).  You can call your primary 
care doctor this week to discuss this medication change.

After speaking with you, it seems that the sadness that you are 
experiencing may be contributing to your symptoms of chest pain 
and taking away some of your desire to eat and drink.  I think 
it is important that you continue to follow up with your 
psychiatrist and try to initiate in home couseling services (per 
your discussion with ___ from our social work service)

We held a few of your medications while you were in the hospital 
since you were getting dizzy when sitting up.  These include 
spironolactone, lisinopril, and amlodipine.  You should continue 
to take your lisinopril, and amlodipine as you were before 
coming in.  We decreased the dose of your spironolactone to 50mg 
twice a day ___ pill twice per day).  You can call your primary 
care doctor this week to discuss this medication change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having these sharp chest pains again, mostly in the middle, and they came on suddenly yesterday. They only last a few seconds, but they scared me. I also felt dizzy when I sat up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was the pain spreading anywhere, like your arm or back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It did go to my left shoulder for a second, but then it stopped. It’s not worse with breathing or moving. I just feel anxious when it happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the dizziness—does it happen when you stand up? Any spinning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially when I go from lying down to sitting. It feels like the room spins for a few seconds. Not all the time, but enough to make me nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and it showed some changes in the heart tracing, but no signs of a heart attack. Your blood tests for heart damage came back normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? I was really worried because it felt similar to last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your normal heart tests and a stress test just six months ago, it’s very unlikely to be cardiac. We also did a chest X-ray. There’s a small area in the back of your lungs that looks a bit collapsed—called atelectasis—but it’s not serious and isn’t causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But why the chest pain and dizziness then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The dizziness seems related to position changes. It’s likely orthostatic—meaning your blood pressure dips briefly when you sit or stand. We gave you IV fluids, and that helped. You haven’t had chest pain since, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, the pain went away after I got to the ER. But I’ve just been feeling… sad lately. Since my mom passed, I haven’t wanted to eat much or leave the house.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry to hear that. You mentioned lack of appetite and low energy. That could be contributing to the dizziness and even the chest pain. Stress and sadness can manifest physically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I never thought it could affect my body like this. I do see a psychiatrist, but maybe I need more support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked social work to help connect you with counseling. Also, your kidney function was a bit off when you arrived—your creatinine was elevated—but it improved quickly with fluids, so that’s resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been stable overnight—no chest pain, and your dizziness is much better. We’re planning to send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about my medications? I noticed some were held.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused lisinopril, amlodipine, and spironolactone temporarily because of the dizziness. You can restart lisinopril and amlodipine as before. But we’ve cut your spironolactone in half—to 50mg twice a day—for now. Talk to your primary doctor about it this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds? I’m worried about my sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glyburide was held yesterday but you’ll restart it at a lower dose—half a tablet twice a day. Keep eating regularly and drink at least four large cups of water daily to prevent dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my migraines? I was on Inderal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You didn’t have any headaches this stay, so that’s good. We’re restarting Inderal as before. But we held it briefly because of the low blood pressure concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are back to normal, and you’ve been walking without dizziness. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors and try to get more help for how I’ve been feeling emotionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great plan. Keep in touch with your psychiatrist, and call your PCP about the spironolactone. Drink fluids, eat well, and take your meds as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in before discharge. Any chest pain or dizziness since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Still a bit tired, but not dizzy or in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, diastolic heart failure, and depression was admitted for recurrent chest pain and dizziness. Initial evaluation revealed transient chest pain with non-specific EKG changes, but serial troponins were negative and prior stress test was normal, ruling out acute cardiac cause. Dizziness was attributed to orthostatic hypotension, likely exacerbated by dehydration and medication effects. Her creatinine was elevated on admission but normalized with IV hydration. Depression was identified as a contributing factor to her symptoms, and social work was consulted for counseling support. Medications were adjusted, including temporary hold of antihypertensives and reduction of spironolactone. She improved clinically, remained asymptomatic, and was discharged home with follow-up plans.
